newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran presidential race boils down to two runners.
newsitem.headline: Iran presidential race boils down to two runners.

text.p: Voters in Tehran are divided over which of two main candidates in Iran's presidential election should shape the future of the Islamic state.
In the most-competitive election since the country's 1979 revolution, the clerical establishment's preferred candidate is facing a real challenge from one of their own.

Parliamentary Speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri still leads in opinion polls over his main rival and former culture minister Mohammad Khatami who, like all four candidates in this election, was allowed to run only after a senior group of clerics and lawyers approved his bid for power.
An opinion poll published in the Iranian Akhbar newspaper on Tuesday showed Nateq-Nouri with 54.63 percent of the popular vote followed by Khatami at 37.42 percent.
Former intelligence minister Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshahri attracted 4.7 percent of the vote and Reza Zavarei, deputy head of the judiciary and only non-cleric in the race, just 1.29 percent.

But despite this poll and a widespread expectation among many of the capital's voters that Nateq-Nouri will be the next president, Khatami can still rely on large swathes of popular support in this city of about seven million people.
"People who come into this shop want a breath of fresh air. They want a change," said Behzad, a middle-aged car parts salesman in a working-class district of south Tehran.
Khatami's supporters say they will vote for him on Friday because of his education, his ability to fight inflation and in the expectation that he will introduce more social freedoms.

"If Khatami wins there will be more cultural freedom, more music on the radio and more diversified programmes on the television. People are tired of being harassed for wearing certain clothing," said Manouchehr, also a salesman.

Those who say they will vote for Nateq-Nouri point to his experience in the country's Majlis, or parliament, and his loyalty to Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the heir to Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini who toppled the Shah.
It is summed up by a young army conscript taking leave from barracks in one of Tehran's rejuvenated public parks.
"Nateq-Nouri is the best of the candidates because he is the most experienced. People know him," said the conscript.
Other backers of the speaker are not difficult to find.

"Personally I will vote for Nateq-Nouri. He's competent and he has been the majlis speaker...He is familiar with the problems of the people," said Hassan Azimi, a grey-haired carpet trader in central Tehran for the past 20 years.
"I look forward that he will get rid of the stagnation we have had in the carpet industry and remove the obstacles (to business)," Azimi said.
Davood Kianbakhsh, a butcher in central Tehran for 40 years, will also be casting his vote for Nateq-Nouri on the grounds of the speaker's past, and his promises on the economy.
"Nateq-Nouri will follow (President Akbar Hashemi) Rasanjani's policies and the future of the country will be bright," said Kianbakhsh in his shop of dead chickens.
Rafsanjani steps down as president after serving the two consecutive four-year terms permitted under the constitution.
Nateq-Nouri supporters might be privately worried about the strength of Khatami's campaign but few are expecting what would be a major upset if Khatami pipped the parliamentary speaker.

In private, Nateq-Nouri supporters accuse Khatami as being a liberal -- a potent slur in this pure Islamic country -- while Khatami voters portray Nateq-Nouri's possible victory as advancing more conservative factions in the regime.

"I will not vote for Khatami because he is an extremist. Iran has been deceived by intellectuals since the early stages of the revolution. If the nation gives itself to the students and intellectuals that is a big blunder," said one shop keeper.
Some of Khatami supporters worry that a Nateq-Nouri presidency will seal power by the more conservative factions over the main institutions of government and society.
"There will be a monopoly if Nateq-Nouri got in. The president and the supreme leader would rule with a conservative majlis. More hardliners would be getting the jobs," one said.
